beats.intro: Chapter seven, lesson one. Phospholipids and the fluid mosaic. [[bubble]]A soap bubble is a thin skin that holds its shape, and yet it flows and shimmers. [[cells]]Every living cell is wrapped in a skin of its own. [[map]]Here is our map of an animal cell, from chapter six. [[lit]]Today we light up one part of it: the plasma membrane, the boundary that separates the living cell from its surroundings. [[push]]Let's zoom in to the edge, and see what it is made of.
beats.edge: A cell is not sealed inside a box. [[gate]]It has to take in food and let waste out, so the membrane works like a border checkpoint. [[select]]It lets some substances cross more easily than others. That property is called selective permeability, and lesson three will explain it. [[why]]First, we need to see the structure that makes it possible.
beats.amphi: The most abundant lipid in the plasma membrane is the phospholipid. [[head]]It has a head that contains a phosphate group. The head is hydrophilic, which means water loving. [[tails]]Hanging from the head are two tails, made of fatty acid chains. The tails are hydrophobic. They hate water. [[both]]A molecule with a water loving part and a water hating part is called amphipathic.
beats.bilayer: Now drop a crowd of phospholipids into water. [[water]]The heads are happy beside the water. The tails are not. [[tuck]]So the tails tuck together, away from the water, and the heads face outward. [[double]]The result is a double layer, a bilayer. One layer faces the extracellular fluid, the other faces the cytoplasm, and the tails of both layers meet in the middle. [[sheet]]It builds itself, with no help from the cell. [[patch]]This sheet is the frame of every membrane in the cell.
beats.q1: Quick check. In a bilayer in water, which part of each phospholipid faces the water?
beats.mosaic: Scientists describe the membrane with the fluid mosaic model. [[fluid]]Fluid, because the lipids are not locked in place. The membrane flows, like that soap film. [[mosaic]]Mosaic, because proteins are embedded in it, like tiles set into a floor, a mixture of different pieces. [[later]]We meet those proteins in the next lesson. Today we stay with the lipids.
beats.move: How do the lipids move? [[lateral]]Most of them drift sideways, within their own layer, swapping places with a neighbour. This lateral movement happens about ten million times every second. Some proteins drift too. [[flip]]But for a lipid to jump to the other layer, its water loving head would have to pass through the water hating middle. This flip-flop is rare, about once per month. [[sum]]So lipids slide freely, but they rarely change layers.
beats.q2: Quick check. Is it lateral movement, or flip-flop?
beats.temp: The fluidity of a membrane depends on temperature. [[cool]]As a membrane cools, it switches from fluid to solid. Membranes must be fluid to work properly. They are usually about as fluid as salad oil. [[sat]]The tails matter. A saturated tail has no double bonds, so it is straight, and straight tails pack tightly. That makes the membrane viscous, less fluid. [[unsat]]An unsaturated tail has one or more double bonds, and each double bond makes a kink. Kinks keep the tails from packing tightly, so the membrane stays fluid. [[rule]]So membranes rich in unsaturated fatty acids are more fluid than those rich in saturated fatty acids, and they stay fluid at lower temperatures.
beats.chol: Animal cell membranes also contain cholesterol, a steroid made of four rings. [[wedge]]It sits wedged between the phospholipid tails. [[warm]]At a warm temperature, like thirty seven degrees Celsius, it restrains the movement of the phospholipids, so the membrane does not get too loose. [[cold]]At a cool temperature, it prevents the tails from packing tightly, so the membrane does not stiffen. [[buffer]]Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer. It keeps the membrane from being too fluid when warm, and too solid when cool.
beats.example: Let's test these ideas on three membranes. [[three]]One is built from saturated tails, one from unsaturated tails, and one is saturated, but has cholesterol. [[chill]]Now chill them. The saturated membrane packs tightly and turns solid first. [[kinks]]The unsaturated membrane, with its kinks, stays fluid for longer. [[chol]]In the third, the cholesterol gets between the tails and blocks tight packing, so it stays fluid too. [[heat]]Now warm them all to thirty seven degrees. The cholesterol holds its membrane back from becoming too loose. [[note]]Different tools, same goal: a membrane that is fluid enough to work, and still holds together.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]The plasma membrane is the boundary of the cell, and it is selectively permeable. [[w2]]Phospholipids are amphipathic, with a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails, so in water they form a bilayer. [[w3]]In the fluid mosaic model, lipids drift sideways all the time, and flip-flop is rare. [[w4]]Kinked, unsaturated tails keep a membrane fluid, straight saturated tails make it viscous, and cholesterol buffers both. [[end]]Now try the practice.
